Per line: N = normalized Akkadian reconstruction (| metrical foot, || caesura); T = eBL English translation; L = lemmas with eBL dictionary glosses; then notes, parallel lines, and the manuscripts' transliterations (ATF). Bibliography keys like [RN117: 889] are resolved in bibliography.md (RN117 = George 2003).

1

  • N: šar (|) gimir (|) dadmē | bānû (|) kibrā[ti (|) ... ]
  • T: King of all settlements, creator of the universe, […]!
  • L: šar ← šarru I “pl. šarrū, šarrānu king”; gimir ← gimru I “totality”; dadmē ← dadmū I “pl. tant. villages, settlements”; bānû ← bānû I “f. bānītu creator, begetter”; kibrā[ti ← kibru I “pl. m. & f. bank, shore, rim of river, canal, sea, as safe place”
  • Note: The interpretation of the opening lines of the poem is a vexata quaestio. The most serious difficulty is the identification of the character described as “king of all settlements,” who could conceivably be Išum, Erra, or even Marduk (see already [RN31: 135-137]). It seems easiest to interpret that the poem begins with a hymn to Išum, as defended by [mueller1995wer: 349-360], [RN1593: 48-49], and [RN455: 60-61], among others. [RN31: 138] assumed that the missing portion of the line contained “un terzo epiteto divino, composto di due o tre elementi, che dia al verso lo stesso ritmo ternario dei vv. 3-5.” [RN675: 263], who is of the opinion that the opening lines are addressed to Erra, restores [qurādu Erra], “[warrior Erra].”
  • Parallels: L 0.0 NA "-" b+1

3

  • N: nāš (|) haṭṭi | ṣīrti | nāqid (|) ṣalmāt (|) qaqqadi | rēʾû | [tenēšēti?]
  • T: Bearer of the august scepter, shepherd of the black-headed people, herdsman of [mankind]!
  • L: nāš ← nāšû I “bearing”; haṭṭi ← haṭṭu II “mostly f.”; ṣīrti ← ṣīru I “exalted, supreme, splendid, outstanding often in stat.”; nāqid ← nāqidu I “pl. m. & f. stock-breeder, herdsman of sheep, goats, cows”; ṣalmāt ← ṣalmāt qaqqadi I “the black-headed ones, i.e. mankind Bab.”; qaqqadi ← qaqqadu I “pl. f. head”; rēʾû ← rē'û I “shepherd, herdsman of sheep, cattle, donkeys, horses, pigs, NA…”; [tenēšēti?] ← tenēštu I “pl. tenēšētu(m), NA tanēšētu people Bab., NA sg. personnel”
  • Note: As noted by [RN83: 22 fn. 3], the entire line contains an etymographic interpretation of the name Hendursaĝa (i.e. Išum): GA₂ = nāš, PA = ḫaṭṭu, SAG = ṣīrtu, PA.<|DAG.KISIM₅×KAK|> = nāqid, SAG GA₂ = GE₂₆ (for GE₆) = ṣalmāt qaqqadi, PA.<UDU> = rēʾû (see also [RN3058: 6a] and [RN1593: 66 fn. 7]). The free restoration tenēšēti at the end follows [temp_id_07390035038145881: 200] (see also [RN31: 140]).

4

  • N: īšum | ṭābihu | naʾdu | ša ana našê (|) kakkīšu | ezzūti | qātāšu | asmā
  • T: Išum, zealous butcher whose hands are suited to bear his fierce weapons,
  • L: īšum ← Išum I; ṭābihu ← ṭābihu I “slaughterer, butcher Bab., NA of animals”; naʾdu ← na'du I “attentive, reverent Bab.”; ša ← ša I “who(m), which”; ana ← ana I “(aš-š... etc.) to, for (freq. abbr. an, with assimilation of n…”; našê ← našû II “to lift, carry”; kakkīšu ← kakku I “stick”; ezzūti ← ezzu I “furious, angry Bab., NA of deity, person, animal, fire, wind”; qātāšu ← qātu I “f.”; asmā ← asāmu I “to be(come) fitting, suitable”
  • Note: As first noted by [RN706: 400] (see also [RN31: 140] and [RN1593: 66 fn. 7]), ṭābihu naʾdu is an etymographic interpretation of the name of Išum. The line is cited in an inscription of Assurbanipal (see [RN661: 192-193] and apud [RN54: 157 l. 22]).
  • Note: Collation of the line in Lambert’s folio 18397.
  • Note: According to [RN31: 140 fn. 11], the sign TA is used for ṭa₂ only in this line in all manuscripts of the Epic.

5

  • N: (u) ana šubruq (|) ulmīšu | šērūti | erra | qarrād (|) ilī | inūšu | ina šubti
  • T: And at the lightning of whose wrathful spears even Erra, the warrior of the gods, trembles in (his) abode!
  • L: (u) ← u I “and, but, also”; ana ← ana I “(aš-š... etc.) to, for (freq. abbr. an, with assimilation of n…”; šubruq ← barāqu I “to lighten, shine Bab.(lit.)”; ulmīšu ← ulmu I “pl. m. & f. (a weapon, phps.) axe M/NA, M/jB, of iron”; šērūti ← šēru I “~ fierce O/jB god”; erra ← Erra I; qarrād ← qarrādu I “pl. also qarrādūtu warlike”; ilī ← ilu I “pl. ilū, ilānu god, deity a or the god, also du.”; inūšu ← nâšu I “to rock, shift Bab., NA”; ina ← ina I “(im-m..., ip-p... etc.) in, on”; šubti ← šubtu I “seat, dwelling”
  • Note: Most modern interpreters take inūšu as a subordinative in the relative clause started in l. 4 (see [RN1593: 66 fn. 6] with further bibliographical references, and also [RN455: 61 fn. 66]). The line is cited in the narrative of Sargon’s Eighth Campaign, as noted by [RN282: 127 fn. 52].
  • Note: Collation of the line in Lambert’s folio 18397.

6

  • N: īrissū-ma | libbašu || epēš (|) tāhāzi
  • T: His heart yearned for combat;
  • L: īrissū-ma ← erēšu II “to request, wish for”; libbašu ← libbu I “inner body”; epēš ← epēšu II “to do”; tāhāzi ← tāhāzu I “pl. f. battle”
  • Note: Compare the description of the passage 6-14 in [RN1593: 49-50]: “The poet follows the five-line invocation by showing Išum (and the audience) a scene in which Išum’s master, lying in bed, ponders the pros and cons of going to war. The arguments are articulated as an internal dialogue between Erra’s mind (libbu, literally ‘heart’) and his physical self.”

10

  • N: attā | dipārum-ma || inaṭṭalū | nūrka
  • T: You alone are the torch, it is your light they look to!
  • L: attā ← attā I “you (2 m. sg. pron.)”; dipārum-ma ← dipāru I “m. & f. torch Bab. d. našû, d. napāhu/nuppuhu to raise, light a…”; inaṭṭalū ← naṭālu I “to look”; nūrka ← nūru I “light of sun etc.”
  • Note: Compare [RN3058: 4a]: “Earlier in the poem of Erra and Išum, Erra’s heart explicitly identifies Išum as diparu, “a firebrand,” that the gods follow into battle (I 10). From this it follows that the light which the night watchmen Išum and Ḫendursanga shone to lead people home at night was a burning torch or firebrand. Indeed, it seems likely that Išum’s divine power was instantiated in the fiery glow of the torch, and that his name was indeed the masculine form of the Akkadian common noun išātum, “fire.””
  • Parallels: cf. L III.4 38

13

  • N: erra | tebī-ma || ina sapān (|) māti
  • T: Should Erra arise, when he destroys the country,
  • L: erra ← Erra I; tebī-ma ← tebû I “OAkk, Ass. tabā'u(m), NB tabû to get up, arise, set out”; ina ← ina I “(im-m..., ip-p... etc.) in, on”; sapān ← sapānu I “to flatten, lay flat Bab., NA”; māti ← mātu I “f. land, country”
  • Note: The line has been almost universally interpreted as a command from Išum to Erra, an interpretation that results in awkward syntax and makes the introduction impossibly difficult to understand. Compare: [RN31: 59]: “Erra, alzati! Nell’abbattere il paese”; [RN447: 117]: “Debout donc, Era! A terrasser le pays”; [cagni1977poem: 84]: “Arise, Erra! By laying waste the country”; [bottero1977antiquites: 113] and [RN39: 682]: “Debout, Erra! Quant tu saccageras la terre”; [RN216: 285] and [dalley1997erra: 405]: “O Erra, rise up, and in overwhelming the land”; [polentz1989eigenbegrifflichkeit: 23]: “Erra, erheb dich! Wie wird beim Niedermachen des Landes”; [RN712: 783]: “Erra, erhebe dich, und beim Einebnen des Landes”; [RN675: 264]: “Erra, erhebe dich! (…) beim Niederwalzen des Landes”; [RN1593: 50]: “O Erra, arise! (…) when laying the land low!”; [taylor2017erra: 336]: “Erra, arise, and in crushing the land”. Note, however, that two MSS (AššNA2 and BabLB1a) have a clear stative tebī-ma, whereas only the Sultantepe MS, whose readings are generally inferior to those of the others, has an apparent imperative ti-be₂-ma. The only interpreter who tried to translate the manuscripts’ stative was [RN1811: 92]: “Ist Era erhoben beim Niederstrecken des Landes”. In our view, it is a conditional sentence (see the note on the next line).

14

  • N: kī namrat | kabtatka || (u) hadû | libbuk
  • T: Your mind will not rejoice, your heart will not be joyous.
  • L: kī ← kī I “like”; namrat ← nawāru I “to be(come) bright, shine”; kabtatka ← kabattu I “liver, also innards”; (u) ← u I “and, but, also”; hadû ← hadû III “to be joyful, rejoice”; libbuk ← libbu I “inner body”
  • Note: As noted by [RN31: 143-144], this is the first line in the Epic in which sentence boundary does not coincide with verse boundary. The plene writing of ḫadû shows that kī cannot be an interrogative adverb, as traditionally interpreted (“wie wird da strahlen dein Gemüt und erfreut sein dein Herz!” in [mueller1995wer: 350]; “How your mood will be bright, your heart joyous!” in [RN1593: 50]); but rather a conjunction introducing an oath formula (“If your mind rejoices and your heart is joyous (…)”, i.e., “your mind will surely not be happy, nor your heart be joyous”).

Il ‘disprezzo’ degli animali (se ne parla solo qui) va interpretato secondo lo stesso ordine di idee e come un topos letterario: anche nella ‘Teodicea Babilonese’ (vv. 45-66) alcuni animali selvatici, che compiono distruzioni, vengono considerati colpevoli di opposizione al culto e pertanto preordinati al castigo.” On the motif, see also [RN984: 69-81].

127

  • N: minsu | šukuttu | simat (|) bēlūtīka | ša kīma kakkab(ī) (|) šamāmī | lulâ | malât | leqât | urūša
  • T: “The image, the ornament of your lordship, which, like the stars of heaven, was full of splendor, why is it covered with filth?
  • L: minsu ← minsu I “why? M/NB(lit.)”; šukuttu ← šukuttu I “adornment, jewellery of women, deities”; simat ← simtu I “appropriate symbol, characteristic before abstr. nouns symbol, proper…”; bēlūtīka ← bēlūtu I “rule, domination Bab., NA b. epēšu to rule”; ša ← ša I “who(m), which”; kīma ← kīma I “like”; kakkab(ī) ← kakkabu I “star also ref. to planets”; šamāmī ← šamāmū I “heavens Bab.(poet.) for šamû I”; lulâ ← lulû I “plenty, luxury, splendour? j/NB l. malû/mullû, šumallû to be…”; malât ← malû IV “to be(come) full”; leqât ← leqû II “to take, take over”; urūša ← urūšu I “? dirtiness jB”
  • Note: The exact translation of šukuttu is debated: some authors prefer a more general translation “jewel” ([RN706: 299]) or “prezioso apparato” ([RN31: 183]), others understand that it refers to Marduk’s statue (so e.g. [cassin1968splendeur: 49 fn. 86], followed by [RN984: 192]). The last word was interpreted as urūšu/urrušu, related to arāšu, “to be(come) dirty” [temp_id_07390035038145881: 205] and as aršu, “dirty,” by [RN31: 183]. [RN2721: U/W 248b] parses it as urrušu, “filthy person or thing.” [RN31: 188] compares the passage with the following lines in an inscription of Esarhaddon ([RN393: Esarhaddon 104 iv 9-17]): “I repaired the woeful desecrated state of the gods and goddess who lived in it, who had been displaced by floods and storm, and whose appearances had become dim; I made their dimmed appearance bright, cleaned their dirty garments, (and) had them permanently installed on their daises.” (DINGIR-MEŠ u {diš-tar a-ši-bu-ut | qer-bi-šu ša₂ A-MEŠ bu-tuq-tu | u₃ ra-a-du u₂-bi-lu-šu₂-nu-ti-ma | i-ki-lu ši-ki-in-šu-un | šal-pu-ut-ta-šu₂-nu lu-mu-un-tu₂ | ud-diš zi-me-šu₂-nu uk-ku-lu-tu | u₂-ša₂-an-biṭ ṣu-bat-su-nu | ar-šu ub-bi-ib ina BARA₂-ME-šu₂-nu | da-riš u₂-šar-me-šu₂-nu-ti}).
  • Note: Collation of the line in Lambert’s folio 18398.
  • Note: ma-la#-at₂# could also be read as ma-la#-ta#

132

  • N: ultu (|) ullu | āgugū-ma | ina šubtīya | atbû-ma | aškuna | abūba
  • T: “Once, in my anger, I arose from my throne, causing a flood;
  • L: ultu ← ištu I “from, out of”; ullu ← ulla II “at some time Bab.”; āgugū-ma ← agāgu I “to be(come) furious Bab.”; ina ← ina I “(im-m..., ip-p... etc.) in, on”; šubtīya ← šubtu I “seat, dwelling”; atbû-ma ← tebû I “OAkk, Ass. tabā'u(m), NB tabû to get up, arise, set out”; aškuna ← šakānu I “to put, place, lay down”; abūba ← abūbu I “flood, deluge Bab.”
  • Note: It is uncertain whether the word abūbu refers to the Flood or to any catastrophe in general. The latter interpretation seems more likely since, as noted by [RN31: 184-186], Enlil is in Mesopotamian mythology the god responsible for sending the flood, and this seems to be the case also in the Epic: in IV 50, it is stated that “Lord of the Lands” (i.e., Enlil) spared Sippar from the Flood, which probably implies that it was also Enlil who sent it. See also [RN801: 251-253, 274-278], who remarks that in the Epic the cause of the Flood is not the overpopulation of the earth. In any case, the subordinative in a-gu-gu-ma and at-bu-ma mean that ultu ullu cannot be taken as an adverbial expression (pace [RN1826: 251-252], “depuis longtemps,” “autrefois”), but rather a conjunction, with [RN27201: §174g*].
  • Note: Collation of the line in Lambert’s folio 18398.

  • L: ina ← ina I “(im-m..., ip-p... etc.) in, on”; šub[t]īya ← šubtu I “seat, dwelling”; atbē-ma ← tebû I “OAkk, Ass. tabā'u(m), NB tabû to get up, arise, set out”; šipīt ← šibītu I “(or šipītu) suture, seam jB in garment, building, skull”; šamê ← šamû I “mostly pl. tant. sky, heaven”; (u) ← u I “and, but, also”; erṣeti ← erṣetu I “earth, land”; uptaṭṭir ← paṭāru I “to loosen, release”

  • L: ša ← ša I “who(m), which”; ina ← ina I “(im-m..., ip-p... etc.) in, on”; tâmti ← tiāmtu I “jB pl. also timiāti sea”; rapašti ← rapšu I “f. rapaš/ltu(m) wide, extended of building, object, road”; (ina) ← ina I “(im-m..., ip-p... etc.) in, on”; mê ← mû I “pl. tant. water mê kabrūtim mass of water”; meʾat ← me'atu I “pl. me'ātu(m), mâtu(m), Mari mêtum (one) hundred as numeral”; bērī ← bēru III “double hour, league”; išissu ← išdu I “pl. f. foundation, base freq. du.”; ikšudu ← kašādu I “to reach, arrive”; šupul ← šuplu I “depth Bab. deepness, š. erṣeti, mê depth of the earth, water etc.”; aralli ← arallû I “netherworld O/jB jB šad a. mountain of the netherworld, also desig.…”
  • Note: The mēsu-tree appears here as axis mundi, as a cosmic tree spanning heaven and earth (see [RN31: 192], [RN220: 28], [stol2017review: 376]). Compare the famous description of the passage in [RN949: 198] (also cited by [RN31: 193]): “Wenn sich im Erra-Epos der senile Marduk darüber beschwert, daß er nach der Sintflut die vorsintflutlichen (im wahren Sinne des Wortes!) mēšu-Bäume, von denen das e[lmēšu] kommt (das Wortspiel mēšu : elmešu ist zu beachten!), nicht wieder auffinden konnte, so wird sicher niemand Bekanntschaft mit den antediluvialen Bernsteinwäldern voraussetzen; wohl aber die halbmythische Vorstellung, daß Bernstein ein Baumharz sei (Plinius zitiert bei Meyer, Konv. Lex.⁵ II 866) bzw. eine Variante der Fabel, daß „Bernstein von Nußbäumen“ stamme (Löw 2, 61 Anm. 1).”
  • Parallels: cf. L I.5 SB "IV" 49

154

  • N: ali | ebbu | zagindurû || ša ušamsakū | uqnâ
  • T: “Where is the pure blue pigment that was made (as) splendid (as) lapis lazuli?
  • L: ali ← ali I “where? OAkk, Ass., O/jB”; ebbu ← ebbu I “bright”; zagindurû ← zagidrû I; ša ← ša I “who(m), which”; ušamsakū ← masāku I “to be(come) bad, worsen Ass., O/jB”; uqnâ ← uqnû I “lapis lazuli”
  • Note: Lambert apud [RN31: 194-195] suggests parsing the verb as nasāqu, “to choose.” Here the interpretation as nasāku, “in Ordnung bringen o.ä.” (so [borger1971tempelbau: 79-80]) is preferred. Although the verb could be a first person, it seems preferable to interpret it as a third person plural, either as an impersonal form, or with the gods that appear in the following lines as its subject. On zagindurû as “Egyptian blue,” see [thavapalan2020meaning: 355-366], with previous bibliography. uqnû, now restored thanks to MS TarNA1, is interpreted as a predicative complement (on this category, see [fromebllab0003: 79-81]); compare II 34: šumsukat eli ša mahri, “I made more splendid than before.”
  • Parallels: cf. L I.5 SB "II" 32

157

  • N: ša kīma ūmi | ušanbaṭū-ma || (ina) šaplūʾa | ukann[u]
  • T: “Who makes (it) shine like the noonday and places (it) at my feet?
  • L: ša ← ša I “who(m), which”; kīma ← kīma I “like”; ūmi ← ūmu I “pl. m. & f. day”; ušanbaṭū-ma ← nabāṭu I “to be(come) bright, shine Bab.”; (ina) ← ina I “(im-m..., ip-p... etc.) in, on”; šaplūʾa ← šaplu II “underside, bottom OB arrears”; ukann[u] ← kânu I “OAkk, Ass. kuānu(m) to be(come) permanent, firm, true”
  • Note: The reading u₂-kan-[na-šu] at the end of the line originates from a suggestion by von Soden (apud [RN1811: 15]). [RN31: 196] cautiously accepted this interpretation and compared it to the common Mesopotamian glyptic motif of a tree “bowed” under the feet of a god. The restoration is, however, highly improbable, as it would produce a non-trochaic ending (ukannašu being a subjunctive). Furthermore, MS TarNA1 appears to allow space for only one sign after kan#. The reading adopted here means that the object crafted by Ninildu is not Marduk’s statue but rather the pedestal upon which the statue rests. There is some evidence of wooden pedestals: for example, an inscription of Esarhaddon describes the reconstruction of the šubat {giš}musukkanni iṣi dārê (“seat of musukkannu-wood, the everlasting wood”) of Tašmētu ([RN393: Esarhaddon 48] r 91; see [RN124: 269]).

165

  • N: [ ... ] ... | [u]ltu? apsî | [ ... ] ... | ana elâti
  • T: “[…] … from the Apsû […] … to the heights.
  • L: [u]ltu? ← ištu I “from, out of”; apsî ← apsû I “(cosmic) underground water Bab., NA”; ana ← ana I “(aš-š... etc.) to, for (freq. abbr. an, with assimilation of n…”; elâti ← elītu I “pl. eliātum, elâtu 'that which is above'”
  • Note: Erra probably promises in this line to bring back up the sages who have gone down to the Apsû. As already assumed by [RN31: 198], ll. 165-167 contain Erra’s response to the problem adduced by Marduk in ll. 147-162: “Mentre il v. 165 è praticamente inesistente, gli altri 2 versi, attraverso i pur scarsi resti (presenza della pietra elmēšu e del verbo (w)aradu) permettono almeno di intuire il contenuto delle parole di Erra. Si tratta della soluzione della seconda difficoltà, sollevata da Marduk in I, 147-ss. Questa interpretazione è sostenuta dall'osservazione sullo svolgimento dell'azione dell'epopea: dopo queste parole di Erra, Marduk non tornerà più sulla sua seconda difficoltà; ritornerà invece a insistere sulla prima (sollevata in I, 128-ss.) nei vv. 170-178 fino a che Erra darà anche a questa una risposta soddisfacente (vv. 182-189).”
